subject: biology
title: Nucleic Acids (HL) Adventure 1: DNA structure and replication enzymes
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet DNA replication at HL depth — every enzyme on the fork.
meta_desc: IBDP Biology HL — DNA replication, helicase, primase, polymerase I/III, ligase, Okazaki fragments.
final_note: You learned DNA replication needs helicase, SSBs, primase, DNA pol III (extension), DNA pol I (primer removal) and ligase to join Okazaki fragments.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Watson, Crick + Franklin (1953): two antiparallel strands, sugar-phosphate backbone, A-T and G-C pairing, ~10 bp/turn.

The strands' antiparallel nature creates a 5' end and 3' end on each — and DNA polymerase only adds 5'→3'.

At each fork:

- Helicase opens the helix at the origin.
- SSB proteins coat single strands.
- Topoisomerase relieves supercoils ahead.
- Primase lays a short RNA primer.
- DNA pol III extends 5'→3': leading strand continuous, lagging in Okazaki fragments.
- DNA pol I swaps RNA primer for DNA; ligase seals nicks.

DNA pol III has 3'→5' proofreading exonuclease — error rate drops to ~10⁻⁷.

Mismatch repair after replication brings final error to ~10⁻¹⁰ per base — 1 mistake per genome per replication.

Telomeres at chromosome ends shorten with each replication; telomerase (active in stem cells, cancer) restores them.

mcqs.q: Which enzyme adds a primer at the origin?
In what direction does DNA polymerase add nucleotides?

numericals.q: Human genome is 3.2 × 10⁹ bp. With proofreading + mismatch repair error rate ~10⁻¹⁰, how many errors per replication on average?

free_texts.q: What name is given to short DNA segments on the lagging strand, named after their discoverer? Two words.
